item.title: What really is the sim-to-real gap?
item.description: Large-scale distributed training runs thousands of worlds per GPU for billions of steps. That is exactly where open-source physics engines quietly break.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR Over the past month we found 20 bugs in open-source physics engines. Most never raise an error. They quietly corrupt what your robot learns in simulation, and show up later as the sim-to-real gap: a robot that works in sim and fails on the real thing.

The worst only appear at scale, the way large-scale distributed training runs: thousands of worlds per GPU, many GPUs, billions of steps. More worlds change the physics, rare poses launch objects, and cables and cloth behave like no real material. We found them in Newton, MuJoCo Warp and MuJoCo, and reported every one upstream.

1. More worlds, different physics#

A ten-cube tower stands on its own. Run it in thousands of worlds at once, and most of the copies fall.

MuJoCo Warp, CG solver: 0 of 16 copies fall, then 92 of 256, 882 of 1,024 and 4,031 of 4,096.

Worlds also leak into each other. In MuJoCo Warp, every world wrote its bounding box to one shared slot, and a ball fell through its own table (#1795; fix #1800 by another contributor).

In Newton’s MPM solver, changing the other worlds moved world 0 by up to 0.1 mm (#5207). And at 4,096 worlds, Newton’s mesh contact buffer filled up without a warning, and pegs sank 28.9 mm into a 20 mm hole.

What it does to training: the more worlds you run, the further your physics drifts from the one world you debugged.

2. Rare poses stop being rare#

In a two-arm task, a 15 mm block resting on a 12.7 mm board was fired straight down through it at several metres per second.

MuJoCo Warp’s general collision routine returned the contact upside down and 27.7 mm deep: both thicknesses added. Its own box-box routine and MuJoCo both say 0.009 mm, pointing up. Only a sliver of heights triggers it:

130 of 2,001 heights, 2 nm apart, all inside 0.35 µm.

What it does to training: a unit test never lands in that band. Billions of steps across thousands of worlds land in it all the time, and the policy learns that blocks sometimes explode. Reported as #1883. Two open PRs from other contributors, #1845 and #1866, together remove every flip on our scan and on 8,000 random poses.

3. The tasks that need scale most get the worst physics#

Cables and cloth are why you need millions of rollouts: they have more ways to move than any rigid object. They are also where the engines are furthest from reality.

Stiff cables sag 40 % too far (Newton, VBD solver1). VBD corrects one body at a time, so a correction crawls one segment per sweep. Our #4795 solves each rod at once and lands within 1–2 % of the exact shape.

A cloth pile sinks through the floor (Newton, VBD with self-contact). 271 of 1,681 particles end up below the ground, the lowest 74 mm down (#5143).

What it does to training: a policy that learns to route a cable or fold a towel, at scale, learns a material that doesn’t exist.

If you train at scale, check this#

  1. Run one scene at 1 and at 4,096 worlds. The physics must match.
  2. Scan awkward poses: thin things resting on each other, shallow overlaps, edges across edges.
  3. Check momentum: push a free object with a known impulse. Its momentum must change by exactly that.
  4. Size contact buffers yourself and check them for overflow every step.
  5. Test soft things at your real mesh size.
  6. In MuJoCo Warp, route box pairs to the box-box routine (turn NATIVECCD off) until #1845 and #1866 land.

What’s next#

These bugs share one cause. The engines are tuned for scenes where a millimetre doesn’t matter, nobody reruns a world, and speed is measured on falling boxes. That is the right tuning for most of their users, and the wrong one for training robot hands at scale. So we are building Alloy, a physics engine for robot hands at scale, around the checks above. It launches soon. Why we are building it, in plain words: Robots need their own wind tunnel.

Footnotes#

Eight more physics bugs. Sketches, not to scale.
Touches 0.1 mm early Spheres and capsules stop 0.1 mm above whatever they land on. Newton · fixed in #4791
One contact, not a line A box lying across another box's edge rests on one contact at its end, not a row. MuJoCo · #3755
16.5 µm read as 190 mm A cylinder barely touching a box gets a huge sideways kick. MuJoCo Warp · fix #1796
Fine cloth won't bend Cloth meshed finer than about 1 mm loses all its bending stiffness. Newton VBD · fix #5131
Small cells, weak bending The finer the mesh, the softer the cloth: 10⁴ times softer at 1 cm cells than at 1 m. Newton XPBD · #5140
Held cloth drops Cloth pinned to a body falls off in deterministic mode. Newton VBD · fixed in #5146
Fluid flows 15 % slow A thin film on the floor drags on the default grid. Newton MPM · #5206
Push 1×, moves 3.2× Pushed cloth flies off 3.2 times faster than the push allows. Newton VBD · #5129

Every report links a script that reproduces it.

References#

  1. Anka He Chen, Ziheng Liu, Yin Yang, Cem Yuksel. “Vertex Block Descent.” ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH), 2024. arXiv:2403.06321. ↩

item.title: Robots need their own wind tunnel
item.description: Physics engines were built for games, controllers and walking. Robot hands need something else, so we are building it.
item.content:encoded:
In 1901 the Wright brothers came home from Kitty Hawk beaten. Their glider lifted far less than their sums predicted. Wilbur said men would fly one day, but not in their lifetime.1

The fault was not in their sums. It was in a number everyone used: Smeaton’s coefficient, 0.005. John Smeaton had worked it out in the 1700s to design windmills.2 It had sat in the books for over a century. Lilienthal used it. So did the Wrights.

So they built a wind tunnel in their bike shop, a wooden box with a fan, and tested some 200 small wings. The real number was about 0.0033, a third smaller.3 Two years later, they flew.

Smeaton’s number was fine for windmills. It was wrong for wings.

Robot learning is in its 1901. Our robots learn in simulators built for something else.

Why simulation matters#

A simulator is a promise: what happens in the box is what would happen outside it.

In 1946 Stanislaw Ulam, recovering from an illness, wanted the odds of winning a game of solitaire. The maths was hopeless, so he imagined playing hundreds of games and counting. That became the Monte Carlo method.4 In 1929 Ed Link built a cockpit tilted by organ bellows. In the Second World War it taught more than half a million airmen to fly on instruments without leaving the ground.5

That is the deal: be wrong for free, many times, before you are wrong for real. Robots take it more than anyone. A simulator runs thousands of copies of a task while a real arm does it once.

The deal only holds if the box tells the truth. A robot trained in a simulator that lies learns a world that does not exist.

What simulators were built for#

  • Games, 2000s. Havok, PhysX, Bullet.6 The job: look right, 60 times a second. A crate a centimetre off is fine if nobody can tell. Getting the same answer twice was hard enough that game developers wrote guides on it.7
  • Controllers, 2012. MuJoCo was built “for model-based control”:8 fast, smooth maths for planners that ask “what if?” millions of times.
  • Walking, 2021. Isaac Gym put thousands of robots on one GPU. A four-legged robot learned to walk in under four minutes.9 Feet on a floor are forgiving.
  • GPU robot learning, 2025. Newton, from Disney Research, Google DeepMind and NVIDIA,10 and MuJoCo Warp. The best open tools we have. We use them every day.

None was built for hands: a plate into a rack, a plug with 0.2 mm to spare, a cable under 2 mm thick, a cloth. None promised the same answer every time.

That is our Smeaton coefficient. Not a bad number. A number made for something else.

What we measured#

We ran the stock engines through 30 test scenes on one GPU and checked each against physics. Three problems stood out.

Same question, different answers. A GPU simulator runs thousands of copies of one world, and the copies stop being copies. A stack of ten cubes stands on its own. Copied 4,096 times, 98 % of the copies fall.

Exact counts: 0 of 16, 92 of 256, 882 of 1,024, 4,031 of 4,096.

A GPU adds thousands of numbers at once, in whatever order its threads finish, and in computer arithmetic order changes the last digit. Only 42 % of GPU setups gave the same result twice. We graded one robot three times, 200 tries each, changing only how its inputs were rounded: it placed the plate 50 % of the time, then 63 %. A ruler that moves 13 points by itself can’t tell you whether a change helped.

Close is not right. Only one stock setup in five passed its physics test. A nut and bolt needed 12–16 % too much twist. A network-cable latch was 9–18 % off.

Fast where it doesn’t matter. A falling body runs at 100 million steps a second. A bin of 64 objects slows every engine to a crawl, and a pile of 256 ran slower on the GPU than on a CPU.

What we fixed#

In three weeks we reported 20 bugs to Newton, MuJoCo Warp and MuJoCo, with 11 fixes. A few:

What broke Engine Status
Round shapes touched 0.1 mm early Newton Fixed
A resting block was fired through its board MuJoCo Warp Fix open
Stiff cables sagged 40 % too far Newton Fix sent
Fine cloth lost its bending, without a warning Newton Fix sent
A cloth pile sank through the floor Newton Reported
Pushed cloth gained 3.2 times its momentum Newton Reported
A held cloth dropped to the floor Newton Fixed
Every world shared one bounding box, and a ball fell through its table MuJoCo Warp Fix open

The physics bugs, animated: Your physics engine breaks at scale

Why upstream fixes aren’t enough#

Newton has merged three of our fixes, two of them within two days. MuJoCo Warp hasn’t merged one in three weeks. That is fair. These engines serve thousands of users, mostly teaching robots to walk, and their maintainers must be careful.

But this is not 20 bugs. It is one pattern: engines tuned for scenes where a millimetre doesn’t matter, nobody reruns a world, and speed is measured on falling boxes. Fixing that one patch at a time is like correcting Smeaton’s coefficient one wing at a time.

So we’re building our own wind tunnel#

The Wrights didn’t stop trusting physics. They stopped trusting a number nobody had checked for their problem, and built the instrument to check it.

We are building a physics engine for robot hands. We call it Alloy: a blend of the best solvers we have taken apart, built on the open work above. Five promises:

  1. Same question, same answer. Bit for bit, for about a quarter more compute, not forty times more.
  2. Right below a millimetre. Plugs, threads, plates, latches.
  3. Thin, soft and tangled things first. Cables, cloth, liquids.
  4. Never wrong in silence. Every copy checks itself, every step.
  5. Fast where hands work. Bins, piles and grasps, not falling boxes.

Alloy launches soon.

References#

  1. U.S. Centennial of Flight Commission. “The Wright Brothers: The 1901 Glider and the Wind Tunnel.” centennialofflight.net. ↩

  2. The Wright Brothers Aeroplane Company. “Kitty Hawk in a Box.” wright-brothers.org. ↩

  3. NASA Glenn Research Center. “Lift Equation of the 1900s.” grc.nasa.gov. The modern value is 0.00326. ↩

  4. Roger Eckhardt. “Stan Ulam, John von Neumann, and the Monte Carlo Method.” Los Alamos Science 15, 1987, pp. 131–141. PDF. ↩

  5. “Link Trainer.” Wikipedia; ASME. “Landmark #210: Link C-3 Flight Trainer.” asme.org. ↩

  6. “PhysX.” Wikipedia. ↩

  7. Glenn Fiedler. “Floating Point Determinism.” gafferongames.com. ↩

  8. Emanuel Todorov, Tom Erez, Yuval Tassa. “MuJoCo: A physics engine for model-based control.” IROS 2012. doi:10.1109/IROS.2012.6386109. ↩

  9. Nikita Rudin, David Hoeller, Philipp Reist, Marco Hutter. “Learning to Walk in Minutes Using Massively Parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning.” CoRL 2021. arXiv:2109.11978. ↩

  10. The Linux Foundation. “Linux Foundation Announces Contribution of Newton by Disney Research, Google DeepMind and NVIDIA to Accelerate Open Robot Learning.” 29 September 2025. linuxfoundation.org. ↩

item.title: Can frontier LLMs fix robots by editing their weights?
item.description: We asked Opus to improve π0.5 by editing its weights directly, with no gradient training. Laundry folding went from 51% to 75%, and a mahjong task from 23% to 36%.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR Robot models like π0.5 show what they are about to do up to a second before they do it, and frontier LLMs can understand these signals. They can also edit, graft and combine the model’s weights directly to make it better, with no gradient training.

We gave Opus 10 manipulation tasks in RoboDojo. It built an algorithm that compares successes with failures to find where each failure lives, then edited just 0.004% of the weights. Success rose on half the tasks, including mahjong (23% to 36%), classifying objects (16% to 21%) and storing a laptop (7% to 12%). When we also let it train small models on simulated trajectories, it found the weight direction that helps folding and lifted folding from 51% to 75%.

Robotics has been built on expensive data collection, complex algorithms and finicky RL. We believe LLMs offer a new way to understand robot brains, optimize them, and eventually solve robotics.

01 · An LLM can read a robot’s brain#

Opus labelled all 73,728 neurons that write π0.5’s motion. In the animation at the top, grab neurons light up to a second before the gripper closes, and release neurons fire as it lets go. Failures show too: on mahjong, the neurons flag a failing grab with an AUROC of 0.81.

How clearly the neurons flag a failing grab, per task

02 · Find the failure, flip it#

Opus compares successes with failures, finds the 128 neurons behind the failure, and flips them: 0.004% of the weights, no gradients.

  1. Record48 stock attempts per task, good and failed.
  2. CompareIn each layer, find the pattern that separates failed grabs from good ones. Check it on held-out attempts.
  3. TargetPick the 2 layers where it is clearest and the 64 neurons in each that write it most.
  4. FlipReverse the pattern in those 128 neurons. Score the edited robot.
failure pattern: the 128 neurons that write it

The biggest win: a mahjong task where the robot lays out three matching tiles to claim four of a kind. Success went from 23% to 36%.

04 · Brain math: copy-paste what a robot learned#

Opus trained two small models on simulated trajectories, one with folding and one without. Their difference is the folding direction. Adding it to the original model lifted folding from 51% to 75%, beating the fine-tuned model it came from.

item.title: Scaling and speeding up robots in the real world
item.description: Three levers that make robot policies run nearly four times faster than the remote-teleoperation data they learned from, without losing accuracy.
item.content:encoded:
Speed is the final frontier that needs to be unlocked before we can see robots assisting humans in the real world.

Speeding up robots is a chicken-and-egg problem: you need deployments in the real world to collect data and iterate on models, but you need fast models in the first place to provide enough economic value to earn those deployments.

Several companies like Physical Intelligence1,2, Skild AI, Generalist AI, Reward AI have shown impressive demos of their models working at impressive speeds, but the fundamental lever behind that is very fast demonstration data, which does not hold once you start scaling a fleet into the real world. We have spent the past few months deploying across various industries, and here is what we, along with several other companies actually deploying robots on the ground, have seen.

Why is deployment data slow?#

Operators in live deployments run two to four times slower than operators in demo setups, for a few key reasons:

  1. Assistance has to be remote to scale. Sending an operator to every site breaks before you reach even a hundred deployments. Remote operation lets one office of trained operators serve many sites without downtime, which makes it the only viable path to human-assisted deployment at scale. Remote teleoperation is slower because it is hard to perceive depth intuitively from camera views; building a 3D environment inside a Meta Quest is a good technical solution, but nobody can use one for more than an hour without feeling nauseated.
  2. The control interface differs. Many demo datasets use leader follower arms3,4, which tie operator speed to physical arm speed. Deployments need dynamic speed adjustment like going slower near humans and fragile objects, for safety, etc. Most deployments we have seen use Meta Quest controllers, which track the operator’s hand and move the arm accordingly.
  3. There is no predictability. Demo scenes are structured and learnable, so operators can act before they think. In a real deployment, an operator has to react to live cues, which is inherently slower.

Why is slow data a problem?#

Slow teleoperation hurts deployment and scaling in two ways:

  1. Weak learning signal. Current robotics policies work by predicting the next chunk of actions. Data in which most of the motion is idle, or does not contain significant movement, carries poor information for a policy to learn from. We have seen this directly in our training runs: policies trained on such data are not only slower but usually less accurate, because each next-chunk prediction offers little progress toward completing the task.
  2. Economics. When a policy or a teleoperator runs significantly slower than a human, it becomes impossible to create economic value for the end customer especially in environments such as kitchens and warehouses, which have been optimised around humans doing tasks quickly and efficiently.

Over the past six months we have run policies in live deployments and focused our engineering and research effort on making policies run faster than the teleoperation data they were trained on, so that we can deploy our robots at scale. We have found three levers that make policies faster while maintaining accuracy:

1. Adaptive speed-up of the training data#

The simplest approach you could think of is to speed up the training data and then train a model on it. Unfortunately, that works poorly in practice: you lose a lot of key information when you discard frames from the data you collect. Uniformly dropping every other frame (2x) took success from 94% to 53%, and at 4x uniform it collapsed to 9% for plate picking, handover between arms and release. The failures concentrated at the grasp and the release, exactly where the discarded frames carried the most information.

A better and more effective approach, also observed by many others in the field, is to treat the motion of the arms as two separate parts: free-space motion, where the arms are travelling toward their target region, and contact-rich motion, where the arms are interacting with the real world. Free-space motion contains far less information about manipulation than contact-rich motion, so it makes sense to speed up free-space motion while keeping contact-rich motion intact.

Prior works such as AutoSpeed5, SAIL6 and SRIL7 have consistently used an RL head to predict contact-rich motion and perform speed-ups around it. We were able to achieve similar or better results without training an RL head at all, by simply treating any motion within x seconds of a gripper event (gripper opening or closing) as contact-rich motion; trying everything from 0.1 to 2 seconds.

We ran hundreds of ablations at 2x, 3x, 4x, 5x and 10x, and across different contact-identification techniques, and saw the best results at 4x with actions within 0.5s of gripper events being classified as contact. Beyond 4x the arm still reaches the object, but it arrives with too much residual velocity to close the gripper cleanly, and success falls off sharply.

Free-space speed-up End-to-end task time vs. teleop data Success rate
1x (raw teleop data) 1.00x 94.2%
2x 1.82x 96%
3x 2.63x 97.4%
4x 3.41x 95.6%
5x 4.02x 82%
10x 6.2x 11%

Contact window fixed at x = 0.5 s; each row is 500 real-robot runs on the same task and scene.

2. Selective chunk skipping at inference#

A VLA policy predicts several chunks of future actions at once. Skipping chunks makes the policy run faster by letting the arm jump to future states, with no retraining. Doing this naively causes two problems, and both of them push the policy out of distribution quickly:

  1. Far-out predictions are less accurate. The further out a chunk is, the less likely it is to be accurate, because the world will have changed by the time the first few actions have been executed. The general practice is to query the model often and execute only near-term chunks.
  2. Skipping causes jitter. When you skip chunks, the arm moves through a different distribution than the training data, and the video feed from the real world no longer corresponds to the training data, which takes the model out of distribution very quickly.

To solve these issues, our approach after running thousands of tests in the real world is to estimate the risk before skipping a step. We look at the motion predicted by the policy and skip only if both of the following conditions hold:

  1. The predicted chunks sit close together in the real world. We measure the end-effector displacement between the last pose of the current chunk and the last pose of the chunk we would skip to, and require it to stay under x cm at 20 chunk executions per second. That threshold is not fixed: a VLM scores the current camera view for scene complexity i.e. clutter, number of movable objects, proximity of a human into 5 buckets, and we scale the allowed displacement from 2 cm in a clean, static scene down to 0.3 cm in a cluttered or human-occupied one. The intuition is that displacement is only safe if the world will still look the way the policy expects when the arm arrives.
  2. There must be no gripper event inside the skipping window.

The second condition is essential. Every time we skipped chunks through a gripper event, the task fell apart. Restricting skips to slow, contact-free motion keeps the policy in distribution. With these techniques we achieve another 22 percent speed-up over our fastest policy.

3. DAgger-style intervention data#

Intervention data is the most useful and most unexpected lever for speeding up a model. We expected it to increase accuracy which it does, at roughly 30x the per-frame value of ordinary teleoperation data. But with no other changes, the policy also gained a 10–15 percent speed-up simply from adding intervention data, sped up using the same techniques described above.

The setup follows DAgger (Ross et al., 2011)8. The policy runs on the robot, and an operator takes control the moment it starts to fail. We then speed up that intervention data with the same gripper-event rule from Lever 1 and retrain.

For models trained at lower speeds, intervention data barely helps with speed, so there is effectively zero speed-up. For policies trained at a faster speed, sped-up intervention data helps them grow faster and faster.

Base policy (training-data speed) + intervention data Success rate Speed vs. base policy
1x — 94.2% 1.00x
1x 200 interventions 96.6% 1.01x
2x — 96% 1.82x
2x 200 interventions 96.2% 1.93x
4x — 95.6% 3.41x
4x 200 interventions 97.2% 3.92x

Final results#

Combined, the three levers let us run our policies nearly four times (3.97x) faster than the data we collected from remote teleoperation. In the table below we report speed alongside accuracy as we add each lever:

Configuration Median task time Speed vs. teleop data Success rate
Teleoperation data (reference) 37.3 s 1.00x 100%
Policy trained on raw data 41.2 s 0.9x 94.2%
+ Lever 1 (adaptive 4x speed-up) 12.1 s 3.08x 95.6%
+ Lever 2 (risk-gated chunk skipping) 9.9 s 3.76x 93.8%
+ Lever 3 (sped-up intervention data) 9.4 s 3.97x 95.2%

Setup. All results are on a bimanual cell of two AgileX PiPER six-DoF arms with parallel-jaw grippers, with three RealSense cameras (one overhead, one per wrist) recorded at 20 fps, driven over CAN from a Jetson Orin NX 16 GB. The policy is π0.52, with an action chunk of 30. Training data is 10 hours of remote teleoperation collected in the same deployment across seven days plus around one hour of usable teleoperation intervention data. Each number in the tables is 500 real-robot runs, with object positions re-randomised between runs.

Limitations#

These results come from a narrow set of tasks: picking up plates and dishes, and picking and placing objects. We have yet to test whether the gripper-event rule and the 4x optimum hold across a more diverse task set. We also have no explanation yet for why 4x outperforms both lower and higher factors.

What comes next?#

We expect our policies to soon run significantly faster than any human can control them, on specific tasks. To build superhuman policies, human data alone cannot get us there.

Human intervention data plays a role in robotics similar to the one RLHF9 played in the early days of LLM post-training. The field had to move past human feedback as models improved, because the models began to outperform expert annotators by too wide a margin. Robotics will hit the same wall in six to eight months.

Our next line of research is RL post-training with no humans in the loop. We plan to apply techniques in the GRPO10 and DAPO11 family to robot policies, with the goal of pushing speed beyond human capability while holding accuracy at similar levels.

References#

  1. Kevin Black, Noah Brown, Danny Driess, et al. “π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control.” arXiv:2410.24164, 2024. ↩

  2. Physical Intelligence, Kevin Black, Noah Brown, et al. “π0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization.” arXiv:2504.16054, 2025. ↩↩
